1955 Ford Fairlane Barned for Decades Hides Tri-Power Surprise Under the Hood
18 photos
Photo: u_ken/eBay
Introduced as a flagship full-size car in 1955, the Ford Fairlane remained in production through 1970. In 1962, it was downsized for the intermediate market, thus becoming part of the muscle car wars.
While the 1960s Fairlane is known for its high-performance credentials (especially when fitted with the R-code 427-cubic-inch V8), the original full-size version is perhaps more famous for introducing the Crown Victoria and 500 nameplates. But that's not to say that it wasn't involved in racing.
The 1950s Fairlane was a common sight in NASCAR, and some of them were also modified for drag racing. The 1955 two-door sedan you see here is one of those cars. Reportedly parked for decades, it still sports a racing livery, while the hood still hides the powerplant that made it run fast across the quarter-mile.
The Fairlane surfaced in Fayetteville, Arkansas, with the seller describing it as a barn find. It's unclear how long it's been in storage, but he says he "was told" that the engine has not run since 1972. Additionally, some paperwork suggests that it may have been titled for the last time in 1967. Well, I guess it's safe to say that it may have been sitting for at least 50 years .
Unsurprisingly, the livery is weathered, and the body shows some rust in places. But it's still in solid condition overall, especially for a vehicle that hasn't been maintained in decades. The interior has seen better days, but it's still complete. Being an old-school drag racer, the Fairlane doesn't have the type of gear you'd expect in a more modern race car (like a roll cage).
The livery states that the engine was built by a guy named John Mahoney, and, indeed, the powerplant is not your average 1955 Fairlane V8. It's a Y-block, which was indeed available in 1955, but its 312-cubic-inch (5.1-liter) displacement makes it incorrect for 1955. This version was introduced a year later.
Moreover, the engine is loaded with performance parts, including an Iskenderian cam, custom headers, and a triple carburetor setup . The latter wasn't available on the Fairlane from the factory. The intake appears to be an Offenhauser unit, which was a common choice for drag racers at the time.
The powerplant mates with a Muncie four-speed manual transmission and a Dana 44 rear end. The Mickey Thompson rear wheels are reportedly original. Unfortunately, the engine doesn't run, and the seller hasn't attempted to revive it. But the V8 turns over, which could mean that it's salvageable without a full rebuild.
The car's odometer reads only 7,854 miles, but there's no confirmation whether it's original or not. The odometer may have turned over once if the car was driven on public roads. On the flip side, it may be one of those vehicles that moved only one quarter-mile at the time. A trophy that comes with the car suggests that the Fairlane remained active at least until 1964.
Although it may not be the most desirable classic dragster out there, this 1955 Fairlane is a cool piece of racing history. If it's something you'd restore or revive as a survivor, the seller wants $10,000 to let it go. What's your take on the price?

source_document.body:
2026 Paris Motor Show • Hyundai Tucson N Line Steals the Spotlight in Paris, but It's All Show and No Go
Honda Canceled Its Entire EV Lineup, but the Alpha Survived and It's Coming Soon
7 photos
Photo: Honda
Honda has officially confirmed that the production version of the 0 Alpha electric SUV will make its debut later this year. The news drops seven months after the Japanese automaker canceled almost its entire electric lineup and completely exited the North American EV market.
Honda scrapped its EV strategy in North America and made the news public in a press release on March 12, 2026. The decision was driven by a major reassessment of its global electrification strategy, due to the EV market meltdown, shifting government subsidy policies, and aggressive competition from Chinese automakers.
Honda was simply unable to deal with all these and canceled the launch of its highly promoted, upcoming in-house-developed electric vehicles that were only months away from going into production at Honda’s Marysville, Ohio, EV hub, retooled based on a massive investment to produce zero-tailpipe-emission cars.
That meant that the Honda 0 SUV , the Honda 0 Saloon, and the Acura RSX EV went straight to the cars' Valhalla without even seeing the light of day in production form. The sudden move led to an estimated $15.7 billion write-off. This adjustment forced Honda to report a net loss for the fiscal year ending March 2026, marking the company’s first annual consolidated operating loss in nearly 70 years.
Photo: Honda Just a few months later, in July 2026, Honda came up with one more cancellation. The automaker announced the complete discontinuation of the Honda Prologue, its only high-volume electric vehicle on sale in North America, by the end of the 2026 model year.
The Prologue sits on General Motors' BEV3 platform, sporting the Ultium battery architecture and sharing its chassis, powertrain, and electronics with the Chevrolet Blazer. The Prologue (still) rolls off the production line of the Ramos Arizpe factory in Mexico, which makes it a victim of the 25% tariffs on imported goods.
The production lines will stop in December 2026. Remaining dealership inventory is expected to completely sell out by the end of the first quarter of 2027. With this move, Honda is exiting the U.S. EV market , as the company fully redirected its resources into manufacturing gas-powered electric hybrids.
However, it turns out that the Japanese automaker still has something to say in the battery-electric car segment and officially confirmed the arrival of the Honda 0 Alpha SUV . Its global debut is set to take place on December 2, 2026, with deliveries starting in early 2027.
Photo: Honda For the moment, prototypes are undergoing road tests in India and Japan. Unofficial reports indicate that the production model will drop the "0 Alpha" designation and receive a new commercial name, set to be revealed shortly.
The model will retain the boxy design with the upright front fascia, supporting the illuminated redesigned "H" logo , a tall roofline, squared-off wheel arches, and flush door handles. A large central touchscreen, a digital instrument cluster, a panoramic roof, and Level 2 ADAS safety systems are expected to make their way on board the Honda 0 Alpha.
Built on Honda's first homegrown, in-house electric skateboard platform developed entirely from scratch, the 0 Alpha, or whatever its name will be, will be available with either the 61-kWh or the 75 kWh battery pack options.
The automaker is targeting a range of up to 404 miles (650 kilometers). However, that sounds overly optimistic. It will more likely be around 280 to 311 miles (450 to 500 kilometers) for the variant with the largest battery pack, in real driving conditions.
Photo: Honda The model will roll off the production line of Honda's Tapakura plant in Rajasthan, India, serving both domestic sales and international exports, including Japan, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Instead of targeting Western regions, Honda is shifting its EV focus, making the 0 Alpha off-limits for U.S. buyers. Why is that happening? It is obviously cheaper to engineer a car to meet the Asian market regulations than to develop it for the American or European markets, where stricter regulations would require a larger investment.
In the meantime, following the multi-billion-dollar EV write-off , Honda is reallocating its North American resources to an aggressive hybrid offensive of next-generation models. Honda is planning to introduce 15 new hybrid models globally by 2030, heavily focusing on North America.
The Ohio EV hub that was originally retrofitted to build the 0 Series EV s will be involved in other projects. Honda is investing $2 billion in an all-new manufacturing facility where it is planning to build a full-size three-row hybrid SUV. This marks Honda's first completely new assembly plant in North America in nearly two decades.
Photo: Honda The firm is still considering introducing EVs in America, but it is stepping back to reconsider its strategy. Seeing how automakers such as Ford, Slate, Hyundai and Kia, and Chevrolet offer affordable zero-tailpipe-emission models, Honda might as well consider joining the segment with a model to start under $30,000.

The new 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic EV has an EPA-estimated range of up to 331 miles, but in the real world, it will likely go even farther.
Mercedes GLC 400 EV beats EPA range in real-world test
Electric vehicles are becoming more efficient thanks to advances in batteries, drive units, and more, enabling longer driving ranges and faster charging.
The new 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic EV has an EPA-estimated range of up to 331 miles, which is more than enough for at least a few days of commuting on average.
In everyday driving conditions, it may drive much farther than its official numbers suggest. During Edmunds’ real-world range test , the GLC 400 EV drove 392 miles, or 18% more than its EPA estimate.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
An extra 61 miles of range is huge. It could add another two, three, or even more days of commuting between charges.
The electric GLC was also more efficient, consuming just 28.4 kWh per 100 miles, about 14% less than the EPA’s official 33 kWh per 100 miles.
Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic with EQ technology (Source: Mercedes-Benz)
Mercedes’ new GLC outperformed most of the competition in the real-world range test. The 2027 Volvo EX60 P10 AWD traveled 352 miles, the 2025 Cadillac Optiq covered 339 miles, and the 2027 Audi Q6 E-Tron Prestige managed 337 miles.
The Edmunds real-world range test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions.
It consists of 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set on auto at 72 degrees.
Mercedes-Benz GLC 400 4Matic with EQ technology (Source: Mercedes-Benz)
While charging speeds weren’t tested, the GLC 400’s 94 kWh battery supports DC fast charging up to 330 kW. Mercedes says it takes about 22 minutes to charge from 10% to 80%.
One thing is for certain: electric cars are quickly becoming more efficient with faster charging and longer driving range.

The number of electric cars offering 300 miles or more of EPA-estimated range has grown from just 1 model in 2016 (the Tesla Model S 90D) to around 60 by the end of 2026.
Several new 2027 models are now pushing closer to 400 miles of EPA range on a single charge. A recent BMW Group study found that Americans want more range than what they actually need.
The study found that 73% say 75 miles or less would cover their daily driving routine, while 42% want at least 300 miles before considering an EV. Only 18% of respondents said they wanted 400+ miles.
